body:
How does a nanosensor work?

A sensor is a device that detects a physical, chemical or biological condition and produces a measurable response. A nanosensor uses nanoscale structures or materials as an important part of this detection process.

For example, a sensing surface may interact with a target gas or chemical. This interaction can change an electrical or optical property of the material. The device then converts that change into a signal.

Because nanomaterials can have a large exposed surface area, many sites may be available for interaction with a target substance. This can improve sensitivity in an appropriately designed sensor.

Sensitivity and selectivity

Sensitivity concerns how well a sensor responds to small changes in the quantity being measured. Selectivity concerns its ability to distinguish the intended target from other substances.

A sensor may be highly sensitive but insufficiently selective. For example, a gas sensor that responds strongly to several gases may not reliably identify one gas without additional features or information.

Applications of nanosensors

  • Medical diagnosis: Detecting selected biological molecules associated with a health condition.
  • Environmental monitoring: Measuring selected pollutants or chemical contaminants in air and water.
  • Agriculture: Monitoring conditions such as moisture or particular chemical indicators to support farm decisions.
  • Food safety: Detecting selected contaminants or biological targets when a validated sensing method is available.

A nanosensor primarily detects or measures a condition. It does not necessarily remove the pollutant or cure the disease that it detects.

Nanotechnology in electronics

Electronic devices depend on materials that control the flow of electric charge. Nanoscale structures can change this control and allow some components to be made smaller or to function differently.

Semiconductor nanostructures

Semiconductors are materials whose electrical conductivity can be controlled under suitable conditions. Silicon is a familiar semiconductor used in electronic components.

Modern microelectronics uses very small structures, including nanoscale features, in the production of certain integrated circuits. Their performance depends on the complete device design and material properties, not simply on making every component smaller.

Quantum dots and displays

Quantum dots are extremely small semiconductor structures whose optical behaviour can depend on size. Under appropriate excitation, different-sized quantum dots of suitable compositions can emit different colours.

This property is useful in selected display technologies where colour quality is important. Quantum-dot displays should not be confused with quantum computers; the two terms refer to different technologies.

Carbon nanotubes and graphene

Carbon nanotubes and graphene have attracted attention because of their electrical and mechanical properties. They are studied for conducting structures, flexible electronics, composites and sensing elements.

Practical use depends on reliability, manufacturing quality, cost and safe handling. A material with excellent properties in a research setting does not automatically become the best choice for every commercial device.

Functional coatings and composites

Nanoscale components can also be incorporated into coatings and larger materials to alter properties such as resistance to wear, interaction with light, or surface wettability. These applications are examples of functional materials: materials selected or modified to perform a particular task.

The distinction between a surface coating, a sensor and an electronic circuit is based on function. All may contain nanomaterials, but they do different things.

Prelims focus

  • Sensors detect a condition and convert it into a measurable response.
  • Sensitivity and selectivity are different performance characteristics.
  • Quantum dots can produce size-dependent optical effects.
  • Graphene and carbon nanotubes are carbon-based nanomaterials.
  • Nanostructures can contribute to semiconductor devices, sensors and functional coatings.
  • Trap: A pollution sensor detects contamination; it does not necessarily remove it.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapters Electricity and Magnetic Effects of Electric Current, for electrical foundations; U.S. National Nanotechnology Coordination Office, About Nanotechnology and Applications of Nanotechnology, sections on electronics, sensors and materials, consulted 13 November 2026; U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, Nanotechnology Frequently Asked Questions, updated 3 March 2026.]

pictures.alt: A target interacts with nanoscale material, changing an electrical or optical property to produce a signal; sensitivity and selectivity are distinguished.
pictures.caption: A nanosensor connects a specific interaction with a measurable response.

title: Nanosensors, Electronics and Advanced Functional Materials

body:
Why does nanotechnology matter for energy?

Energy technologies convert, store or transmit energy. The materials used in these systems influence how efficiently they work and how long they remain useful.

Nanotechnology can improve selected material properties, such as surface area, light absorption or movement of electrical charge. However, nanomaterials do not create energy from nothing; they can only improve particular stages of energy conversion, storage or use.

Solar energy

Solar cells convert light energy into electrical energy. Nanostructured materials may help a solar device absorb light or transport electrical charges more effectively. Certain nanoscale coatings may also help modify how light interacts with a surface.

Such improvements depend on the complete device. A nanomaterial that absorbs light efficiently does not necessarily produce a highly efficient solar cell unless the other parts of the device also perform well.

Batteries and energy storage

Batteries store energy in chemical form and deliver electrical energy during discharge. Nanostructured electrode materials can provide more reaction surface or shorter distances for the movement of charge-carrying ions.

Potential benefits include changes in charging behaviour or storage performance. But a larger reactive surface can also increase unwanted side reactions in some systems. Battery performance must therefore be assessed as a whole, including safety and useful life.

Catalysts and clean-energy processes

A catalyst increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being consumed overall in the reaction. Nanocatalysts may offer many accessible active surface sites because of their small size.

Nanocatalysts are studied for selected reactions in fuel cells, hydrogen-related processes and pollution-control equipment. Their efficiency depends on composition, operating conditions and durability.

Nanotechnology in water treatment

Water can contain suspended particles, disease-causing organisms, dissolved salts, metals and organic contaminants. Different contaminants require different treatment methods. Nanotechnology contributes materials for separation, adsorption, chemical treatment and sensing.

Nanofiltration and specialised membranes

A membrane is a barrier that allows some substances to pass through while restricting others. Nanofiltration is a pressure-driven membrane separation process that can retain selected dissolved substances, particularly certain larger dissolved molecules and multivalent ions.

Its name describes a membrane separation method; it does not mean that free nanoparticles must be mixed into the water.

Reverse osmosis uses a different, generally tighter membrane separation process and is widely used when substantial removal of dissolved salts is required. Nanofiltration does not automatically make saline water completely salt-free.

Adsorption using nanomaterials

Adsorption occurs when molecules or ions attach to the surface of another material. Nanostructured adsorbents can provide a large accessible surface for capturing selected contaminants.

For example, suitably designed materials may adsorb certain dye molecules or metal ions. Adsorption transfers the contaminant from water to the adsorbent; it does not necessarily destroy the contaminant. The used adsorbent must be managed appropriately.

Photocatalysis and antimicrobial treatment

Photocatalysis uses light-activated catalysts to promote chemical reactions. Suitable titanium dioxide materials can help break down certain organic pollutants under appropriate illumination and operating conditions.

Some nanoscale materials also show antimicrobial activity. However, removing microorganisms, removing dissolved salts and breaking down chemical pollutants are separate treatment objectives.

Improved water-treatment performance is not sufficient if treatment introduces harmful nanoparticles into the finished water. The possible release of treatment materials, the quality of the treated water and the handling of spent materials all require consideration.

Energy and water: a shared environmental issue

A nanomaterial may improve an energy or water-treatment device during use but require substantial resources during manufacture. Its overall environmental benefit cannot be concluded from operating performance alone. The complete life cycle must also be considered.

Prelims focus

  • Nanostructures can modify light absorption, electrode behaviour and catalytic activity.
  • A catalyst speeds a reaction without being consumed overall.
  • Nanofiltration is a membrane separation process.
  • Adsorption captures substances on a surface; it does not necessarily destroy them.
  • Photocatalysis requires an appropriate light-activated catalyst and suitable conditions.
  • Trap: Nanofiltration and reverse osmosis are not identical, and neither treatment should be assumed to remove every possible contaminant.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 6, Chapter Water, printed pp. 136-138; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter Sources of Energy; U.S. National Nanotechnology Coordination Office, Applications of Nanotechnology, sections on energy and environmental applications, consulted 13 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Nanomaterial properties support different functions in energy technologies.

pictures.alt: Nanofiltration and reverse osmosis separate contaminants, adsorption captures them on a surface, and photocatalysis promotes organic contaminant breakdown.

title: Nanotechnology in Energy and Water Purification

body:
Why is nanotechnology considered for agriculture?

Plants require essential nutrients, water and suitable growing conditions. Conventional agricultural inputs can be effective, but part of an applied nutrient may not reach the crop. Depending on soil conditions and application methods, nutrients can be lost through leaching, runoff or other processes.

Nanotechnology is investigated to improve nutrient delivery, control the release of selected agricultural substances and monitor field conditions. These are different applications and should not be treated as one technology.

Nanofertilisers

A nanofertiliser is a fertiliser product in which nanoscale materials or nanoscale formulations contribute to nutrient delivery or product performance. Its exact composition and action depend on the formulation.

Plants need several nutrients. Among the major nutrients, nitrogen (N) supports the formation of proteins and other essential plant compounds, while phosphorus (P) is important in energy transfer and growth processes. Potassium (K) is another major plant nutrient.

Nano Urea and Nano DAP

ProductMain nutrient connectionEssential distinction
Nano UreaNitrogenDesigned to supply nitrogen through its particular formulation
Nano DAPNitrogen and phosphorusProvides a different nutrient combination from Nano Urea
Conventional ureaNitrogenConventional nitrogen fertiliser, not automatically identical in application or performance to Nano Urea
Conventional DAPNitrogen and phosphorusConventional fertiliser with a different formulation and application context from Nano DAP

DAP stands for diammonium phosphate. Both conventional DAP and Nano DAP are associated with nitrogen and phosphorus nutrition, but their chemical presentation and recommended methods of use may differ.

How can nanofertilisers affect nutrient delivery?

Some nano-based fertiliser formulations are intended for foliar application, where nutrients are applied to plant leaves. Others may be used through different approved methods, depending on the specific product.

Smaller particles or engineered formulations can influence surface contact, dispersion and nutrient release. However, actual uptake depends on the crop, growth stage, weather, soil nutrient status and application method. A theoretical improvement in nutrient delivery is not the same as a demonstrated increase in yield under every field condition.

A nanofertiliser should not be assumed to replace every quantity of conventional fertiliser in every crop. Replacement or reduction claims must be interpreted according to the specific product, approved recommendations and field evidence.

Gujarat: Nano Urea production at Kalol

Gujarat has a direct connection to the production of nano-based agricultural inputs. On 28 May 2022, a Nano Urea (Liquid) Plant constructed by the Indian Farmers Fertiliser Cooperative Limited (IFFCO) at Kalol, Gujarat, was inaugurated.

This is an identifiable example of nanotechnology-related agricultural manufacturing in Gujarat. It should not be confused with the launch date of India's broader national nanoscience programme.

Regulation and field evidence for Nano DAP

India's Fertiliser (Control) Order, 1985, provides a regulatory framework covering specified fertiliser products. In an official statement dated 6 August 2024, the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers reported that Nano DAP had been notified under the Fertiliser (Control) Order, 1985 on the basis of bio-efficacy trials and toxicology tests.

The same statement reported that preliminary trials involving selected crops indicated the possibility of saving some conventionally applied granular DAP through Nano DAP use. The finding was presented as a possibility based on selected trials, not a universal statement that all granular DAP could be eliminated.

Other agricultural applications

  • Nanosensors: Can help monitor selected soil, water or crop conditions.
  • Nanopesticide formulations: May be designed to improve delivery or control release of an active substance, but performance and effects on non-target organisms must be evaluated.
  • Protective materials: Certain nanostructured coatings and packaging materials may have useful properties for agricultural supply chains.

Nanofertilisers and genetically modified crops are different concepts. A nanofertiliser supplies or carries nutrients; genetic modification deliberately changes genetic material. Use of a nanofertiliser does not, by itself, make a crop a genetically modified organism.

Prelims focus

  • Nano Urea is associated with nitrogen nutrition; Nano DAP is associated with nitrogen and phosphorus.
  • DAP stands for diammonium phosphate.
  • The IFFCO Nano Urea (Liquid) Plant at Kalol, Gujarat, was inaugurated on 28 May 2022.
  • India's Fertiliser (Control) Order dates from 1985.
  • A government statement of 6 August 2024 reported Nano DAP's notification under that Order.
  • Trap: Preliminary evidence of possible conventional fertiliser savings is not proof of universal, complete replacement.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter Crop Production and Management, printed pp. 5-7; Press Information Bureau, Prime Minister's Office, PM addresses a seminar of leaders of various cooperative institutes in Gandhinagar, 28 May 2022; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, Government of India notifies Nano DAP under Fertilizer Control Order, 6 August 2024; official releases consulted 13 November 2026.]
